To structure a presentation: tout d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin, pour conclure.
To explain and add ideas: en effet, d’ailleurs, en outre, de plus.
To contrast ideas: cependant, pourtant, en revanche, par contre.

Monday, 15 January, ten o’clock, the meeting room at Atelier Rhône. Radu presents his sketch for the La Duchère rehearsal room to Claire Vasseur, Nathalie and Ioana.
Madame Vasseur, thank you for coming. First of all, I’m going to present the site, then the project, and finally the budget.
The site is next to the school. It’s small, but very well located. Indeed, the children won’t need to cross the road.
That’s important. Besides, the parents have asked me for that several times.
Next, the project. We’ve planned two rooms: a large one for the orchestra, a small one for individual lessons. In addition, there’s a space for storing the instruments.
(smiles) They have their corner, of course. The windows are smaller than in my first sketch. Consequently, the room will stay cool in summer.
Very good. However, I have one concern. The region’s budget is limited. Isn’t two rooms too expensive?
That’s the last part. Two rooms cost twenty per cent more than one. On the other hand, we’re using local wood, which reduces the cost of construction.
In total, we stay within the budget, provided we start work before the summer. To conclude, I’d say it’s a good compromise between your needs and your constraints.
(looks at Nathalie) You’ve trained him well in a week.
It wasn’t Nathalie. It was my tutor. She made me start again three times.
Well, your tutor was right. In short, I approve the project. Work has to start in April. Can you manage that?
Yes, Madame. One last thing, however: in front of the entrance there will be a bench. And a lime tree. That’s not negotiable.
made ("faire recommencer" = to make someone start again)
"Suh-pahn-dahn": two nasal "ahn"s, the e in "ce" is barely heard.
"Kohn-say-kahn": nasal "ohn" at the start, "ahn" at the end.
A well-organised presentation or text in French announces the order of its ideas. The French value this structure (le "plan") very highly, at school and at work:
tout d’abord, d’abord, premièrement, pour commencer
pour conclure, en conclusion, bref, en somme
Don’t confuse "enfin" (finally, the last item of a list) with "finalement" (in the end, the outcome of a development): "Finalement, il a accepté." = In the end he accepted.
Il est bien situé. En effet, les enfants ne traversent pas la rue.
C’est important. D’ailleurs, les parents l’ont demandé.
En outre, il y a un espace pour les instruments.
"En effet" doesn’t mean "in effect"! It means "indeed", "because", and introduces an explanation. It’s one of the most common connectors in written French.
Il a beaucoup travaillé ; pourtant, il a échoué.
C’est plus cher. En revanche, le bois est local.
C’est beau. Par contre, c’est cher.
Il est petit, mais bien situé.
"Cependant" and "pourtant" contrast an idea with what we would expect. "En revanche" compares two aspects: one negative, one positive.
The windows are smaller. Consequently, the room will stay cool.
We use local wood. Thus, the cost is reduced.
In short, I approve the project.

Punctuation: connectors at the start of a sentence are followed by a comma: "Cependant, …", "Par conséquent, …". Between two clauses, a semicolon is often used: "Il pleut ; par conséquent, nous restons."

On Saturday 3 February, at ten o’clock, the covered playground of the La Duchère school was full. All the children from the orchestra were there, with their parents, brothers, sisters, and even a few grandparents. On a board, Radu had pinned up the plans of the future room, printed in very large format.

He had prepared his presentation as he had for Claire Vasseur, with a three-part plan. But after three minutes he realised nobody was listening. The children had stood up and gathered in front of the drawings, noses pressed to the paper, arguing about where their place would be.

Ioana, sitting at the back, smiled. She got up and came over to her brother. "Change your method," she whispered. "Don’t explain the project to them. Ask them what they want." Radu hesitated for a second, then put his notes down on the table.

"Right," he said. "Forget everything I’ve just said. First of all, I’d like to know one thing: if you could have anything at all in this room, what would you want?" There was an astonished silence. Then a forest of hands went up.

A little boy of seven, the youngest in the orchestra, asked for a slide to get down from the stage. A girl wanted purple walls. Another asked for a fridge full of ice cream. The parents laughed. Radu wrote everything down, very seriously, in a big notebook, as if these were official requests.

Then the requests became more serious. Yanis raised his hand. "I’d like a window up high, in the roof. To see the sky when we play. In here we can only see the wall of the gym." Radu looked at Ioana. Ioana nodded. It was a good idea, and it wasn’t expensive.

Inès asked for something nobody had thought of. "There should be a comfortable chair in the front row. A real one, with armrests. For Madame Roux. The school chairs hurt her back. Besides, she isn’t the only one." Several grandmothers applauded at the back of the room.

Madame Mansouri raised her hand in turn. She asked, rather shyly, whether it would be possible to have a small room for the parents, with a coffee machine, so they could wait for the children in winter without standing in the cold. "My husband finishes his night shift at six. Indeed, he comes straight to pick up Yanis."

Radu noted it down. Then he drew, there and then, with a marker, on the big plan pinned to the board: a window in the roof, a little waiting room by the entrance, an armchair in the front row. The children watched the drawing change before their eyes, fascinated, as if watching a magic trick.

However, when the seven-year-old asked again for his slide, Radu had to say no. "The slide isn’t possible. On the other hand, I can promise you one thing: next to the bench, under the lime tree, there’ll be plenty of room to play." The boy thought about it, then accepted the compromise with the dignity of a minister.

At the end of the meeting, Monsieur Mansouri, who hadn’t said anything, came over to Radu. He looked at the plans for a long time. Then he put his finger on the window in the roof. "Back home, in the village," he said, "we used to play music outside, under the stars. My son doesn’t know that. Thank you for giving him a piece of sky."

The following weeks were devoted to the least poetic part of the project: the planning permission file. Radu had never imagined that such a small building could require so much paperwork. There had to be elevation drawings, sections, a safety statement, an accessibility study, a twelve-page form.

The form was written in a language Radu called "administrative French". All the sentences were nominal: "Declaration of the opening of the site", "Certification of compliance with accessibility rules", "Application for exemption". He spent a whole evening translating the form into normal French, with Chloé’s help.

Chloé had become a precious ally. She didn’t say much, but she knew all the standards by heart. When Radu forgot an emergency exit or drew a staircase that was too steep, she would quietly stick a yellow post-it on his screen with a single word: "Standard?" Radu had ended up calling these little notes "Chloé’s warnings".

On 28 February, at five o’clock, Radu submitted the file at the town hall. It was so thick it had taken two binders. The lady at the counter looked at him with pity. "First planning application?" Radu nodded. She smiled. "There’ll be others. You never forget the first one."

Meanwhile, at home, Rose-Hélène would soon be one. She crawled everywhere at an impressive speed, and stood up as soon as she found something to hold on to. But she stubbornly refused to let go. As soon as you held out your hands to encourage her to walk, she sat back down on the floor, looking offended.

"She’s waiting," Julien said one evening. "Hélène asked her to wait for her, remember?" Ioana laughed, but deep down she wasn’t so sure. Hélène was more and more tired. She hardly left her room any more, and on Wednesdays, when Julien came to visit, she often fell asleep in the middle of the conversation.

And yet she wanted to know everything about the project. Every Wednesday she asked for news of the permit, the children, the lime tree. Julien brought her photos of the plans, and she looked at them through her magnifying glass for minutes on end. Once, she asked whether the lime tree could already be chosen. Julien promised to talk to Radu about it.

Radu, for his part, had another project, a much more secret one. One evening in February he turned up at Ioana’s unannounced, while Lucia was at a flamenco class. He sat down in the kitchen, refused the tea, and took a small blue velvet box out of his pocket.

Ioana’s eyes widened. In the box was a very simple silver ring with a small red stone. "It belonged to our great-grandmother," said Radu. "Mum sent it to me last week. I want to ask Lucia to marry me at Easter. In Seville, in front of her grandfather."

Ioana put her hand over her mouth. Then she hugged her brother so tightly that he protested. Julien, who had been listening from the living room, came to join them with Rose-Hélène on his shoulders. "First of all, congratulations," he said. "Next, if you need any advice on the proposal, I have some experience."

"Under a walnut tree, with a ring hidden in a suitcase full of scores," Ioana specified, laughing. "And after first asking my father’s permission, on the balcony." Radu smiled. "Exactly. I have to ask Lucia’s grandfather for permission. And he only speaks Spanish. And he’s very, very strict."

"Consequently," Julien concluded, "you have to learn Spanish in six weeks." Radu groaned. Ioana burst out laughing. Rose-Hélène, from her father’s shoulders, grabbed her uncle’s hair and shouted something that sounded vaguely like "Rara". It was, apparently, her second word.

The next day, Radu downloaded an app to learn Spanish. He practised on the bus, during his lunch break, in the evening before going to sleep, behind Lucia’s back. When she caught him murmuring "Señor, quiero casarme con su nieta", he claimed to be revising for a language exam. Lucia didn’t believe him for a second, but she pretended.

On 4 March, Rose-Hélène turned one. They had a little party at home: Odile, Radu, Lucia, Karim, Leïla and their daughter, and the grandparents from Annecy, who had come for the weekend. Sophie had made a piano-shaped cake. Rose-Hélène put both hands in it before anyone had even lit the candle.

Hélène hadn’t been able to come. The doctor had forbidden outings for a few weeks. So in the afternoon, the whole family went up to Fourvière with the rest of the cake. Hélène was waiting in her armchair, made up, her hair done, in her best dress. She looked tiny in her big armchair, but her eyes were shining.

Ioana put Rose-Hélène down on the floor in the middle of the room. The little girl stood up, holding on to the bed. She looked at Hélène, two metres away. Hélène held out her arms. "Come, darling. I’m here. I’ve waited for you." The room fell silent. Everyone held their breath.

Rose-Hélène let go of the bed. She wobbled. She took one step, then a second, arms out like a tightrope walker. At the third step she nearly fell, then caught herself. At the fifth, she fell into Hélène’s arms, laughing her head off. Her first steps. For Hélène. Just as she had promised.

Nobody said anything for a long time. Brigitte was crying. Odile was crying. Pierre was pretending he had something in his eye. Hélène held the little girl close, her eyes shut, murmuring something nobody could hear. Then she looked up at Julien and Ioana and smiled.

"One thing done," she said. "Now there’s Radu’s room left." Radu came forward. He had news to announce. "The town hall called this morning," he said. "The permit’s been granted. The foundation stone will be laid on Monday 15 April." Hélène closed her eyes for a moment. "The 15th of April," she repeated. "I’ll be there."

Coming down from Fourvière that evening, Ioana took Julien’s hand in the funicular. Rose-Hélène was asleep in the pushchair, worn out by her five steps. Ioana said nothing. Neither did Julien. They were both thinking the same thing, and neither of them dared say it out loud.

In the end it was Julien who spoke, very softly. "She said: one thing done." Ioana squeezed his hand. "I know." Then she added, after a long silence: "Then the room has to be built very quickly." Through the funicular window, the lights of Lyon went by, one by one, like notes on a score.
